I’ve lately fallen in love with walking with no destination. No podcast, no pace goal, just shoes and weather and time to spare. It started as a way to clear my head after long days staring at screens, but it’s become something closer to a practice, a small daily devotion to noticing.

Yesterday I noticed how much of the world is rebuilding itself. A sidewalk crack sprouting clover, a sparrow bathing in a puddle, a neighbor’s lemons leaning heavy over a fence. None of it was spectacular, and that was the point. Beauty without performance feels like a gift for whoever slows down.

Walking does something to thoughts, too. Problems that feel knotted at a desk start to loosen after a mile. I’ll turn a sentence over in my mind, or replay a conversation, and suddenly the kinder interpretation arrives, or the simpler solution. But I just know my best ideas show up around corner three, out of breath and uninvited.

I’ve also started waving at people more. Just a nod to the mail carrier, a smile for the kid on training wheels. Cities can feel lonely even when crowded, and tiny acknowledgments stitch us back together. Most people smile back, surprised, like they’d forgotten that was allowed.

If you’re feeling stuck or a little blue, borrow my prescription: twenty minutes, no phone, look up. Count colors, listen to the wind, let your mind wander. You don’t have to solve anything. Just come home more human than when you left.
